title: OpenCode Accused of Delaying Breach Alert as User Crypto Stolen

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
A security researcher alleges that the coding agent OpenCode waited until 21:00 UTC on Oct. 17 to instruct customers to rotate security keys, despite knowing those keys were decryptable roughly 14 hours earlier. According to the researcher, known as tayvano, OpenCode contacted external providers including Stripe and OpenAI to revoke compromised secrets by 09:00 UTC, yet cryptocurrency stored alongside user keys began being drained at 19:00 UTC. Tayvano claims the company prioritized revoking keys through third parties over notifying the users themselves.

The security breach impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users who had linked accounts with external providers. While OpenCode attributed the event to a "large scale distillation attack" on a legacy system, some users reported financial losses between $400 and $1,700. OpenAI has since refunded credits drawn during the attack, a move Fortune described as a first for the company, although Anthropic and Google have not announced similar refunds for charges run up on their keys.

selectedTweets.text:
- obviously IR has worked without AI for decades. your response process shouldn't completely rely on praying a commercial api won't refuse you mid-incident. you also have options… at least keep open models in your fallback stack.
- dumping raw malicious code and logs into an agent asking “we got hacked, what do we do” is guaranteed to trigger refusals. hire actual security engineers… they know how to break down the investigation step-by-step so you don't trip safeguards.
- that said, anthropic and openai safeguards are still insanely annoying and sometimes trigger even on basic “fix this” queries.
- trusted access programs need to do way better… daybreak blue still only gives reduced refusals on older models, leaving out newer models like 6.1-sol and astra (not to mention the mess around the approval process, naming, and access tiers).
